frozen_original.title: Linda McMahon Cuts Education Department Staff by 45%, Transfers Programs Without Authorization
frozen_original.synopsis: Education Secretary Linda McMahon oversaw a reduction of Department of Education staff from roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 to 2,300 — a 45% cut. More than 100 programs and department obligations were offloaded to other federal agencies, including elementary and secondary education programs moved to the Department of Labor and family engagement efforts transferred to HHS. McMahon testified before a House Education hearing: "It is the mission to shut down the bureaucracy of the Department of Education." The proposed FY2027 budget called for a $12 billion (15%) reduction in education funding. McMahon's strategy involved making all interagency transfer agreements temporary to shield them from legal challenge. Democrats accused McMahon of "dismantling one of the country's strongest civil rights institutions."
frozen_original.rationale: Systematic dismantlement of the Education Department — transferring programs without congressional authorization, slashing staff, cutting funding — undermines educational equity for millions of children. The deliberate strategy of making transfers "temporary" to evade legal accountability reveals awareness these actions may be unlawful.

events.title: Gabbard Removes Two National Intelligence Council Leaders
events.description_short: Gabbard Fires National Intelligence Council Acting Chairman and Deputy (May 2025).
events.description_medium: Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and deputy Maria Langan-Riekhof in May 2025, according to The Washington Post. The removals followed an assessment that contradicted the administration’s stated rationale for deportations; their direct role in drafting that assessment was unclear. The assessment was dated April 7 and was later partially declassified.
events.description_long: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and his deputy, Maria Langan-Riekhof, in May 2025, The Washington Post reported. Their departures came about a week after the council produced a partially declassified assessment stating that Venezuela’s government was most likely not directing the Tren de Aragua gang’s activity in the United States. That assessment undercut a rationale the Trump administration had used for invoking the Alien Enemies Act to deport alleged gang members. The Post said it was unclear whether Collins or Langan-Riekhof had a direct role in preparing the assessment, which was attributed to a National Intelligence Officer for the Western Hemisphere. The intelligence office spokesperson said Gabbard was working with Trump to end politicization of the intelligence community; lawmakers criticized the removals and warned they could chill independent analysis. The event should be stated as personnel removals following the report, while avoiding a definitive causal claim absent documentation.

events.title: CIA Fires an Unspecified Number of Probationary Recent Hires
events.description_short: Reuters reported the CIA fired more than a few probationary recent hires in early March 2025; the agency did not disclose a count.
events.description_medium: In early March 2025, the CIA fired an unspecified number of probationary recent hires, Reuters reported. The agency said it was reviewing employees in their first two years; an unnamed source said congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when dismissals began. Reuters said the dismissals began earlier that week and affected more than a few hires.
events.description_long: The CIA terminated a number of recent hires in early March 2025 as part of a review of probationary employees, Reuters reported. Three people familiar with the matter said the dismissals affected more than a few employees, but the agency did not disclose a total. A CIA spokesperson said the agency was reviewing personnel in their first two years of service and that some reviews would result in termination. The employees worked across several portfolios, and a person familiar with the matter cited performance issues as the stated basis for some terminations. Reuters also reported, based on an unnamed source, that congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when the dismissals began, despite such notification being customary. The agency’s announcement supports a discrete staffing action, but the article does not verify a specific number or that all probationary officers were fired. The held language “mass firing” overstates the public evidence; claims about required notification and national-security effects should be attributed to the cited source or experts.

events.title: Gabbard Revokes Security Clearances of 37 Officials
events.description_short: DNI Gabbard revoked clearances of 37 current and former officials; a senior CIA Russia analyst lost hers four days after the Alaska summit.
events.description_medium: On August 19, 2025, Gabbard revoked clearances for 37 officials; a senior CIA Russia analyst lost hers four days after the Alaska summit, The Washington Post reported. The memo cited alleged politicization, safeguarding failures or departures from professional standards, but did not list an individual infraction for every person named.
events.description_long: The Washington Post reported that Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard’s August 19, 2025 memorandum revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former officials. The memo cited alleged politicization of intelligence, failures to protect classified material or departures from professional standards, but did not identify specific infractions for every person named. Four days after the Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, a senior CIA Russia analyst was ordered to surrender her clearance, according to the Post. She had served in public intelligence work for 29 years and had an approved assignment in Europe; the clearance action ended that career. The Post reported that she had helped prepare the administration for the summit, but the reporting does not establish that the summit itself caused the revocation. The memo’s broader list and the separately reported effect on the analyst should remain attributed to the Post, and no individual misconduct should be implied absent evidence.

events.title: Trump Announces U.S. Withdrawal from Paris Climate Agreement
events.description_short: On June 1, 2017, Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Agreement; the announcement began a process rather than ending U.S. participation that day.
events.description_medium: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the 2015 Paris Agreement, saying he believed it disadvantaged U.S. workers and businesses. He said the administration would seek to negotiate a new or revised arrangement. The announcement began a withdrawal process; it did not end U.S. participation that day.
events.description_long: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the 2015 Paris Agreement, the international framework through which countries submit climate goals and report on efforts to limit warming. In his Rose Garden remarks, Trump said the deal disadvantaged U.S. workers and businesses and declared that he had been elected to represent Pittsburgh rather than Paris. He said the administration would stop implementing its emissions target and seek to negotiate a new agreement or rejoin on terms he considered fairer. The announcement began a formal withdrawal process; it did not immediately end U.S. participation in the treaty. The announcement and the treaty’s later effective withdrawal date are distinct events. The reviewed official statement supports the date, the stated economic rationale and the administration’s stated next step. It does not establish that the United States was the only country outside the pact or that the announcement was a “devastating blow” to climate diplomacy. Those unsupported or evaluative claims are omitted.

source_to_fact.supports: June 1 announcement, Trump’s stated economic rationale, intended withdrawal and stated next step.

events.title: Trump Says He Directed DOJ to Terminate Remaining Biden-Appointed U.S. Attorneys
events.description_short: On February 18, 2025, Trump said he had instructed the Justice Department to terminate the remaining U.S. attorneys appointed by Joe Biden.
events.description_medium: Reuters reported that Trump announced the instruction in a Truth Social post, saying he wanted to “clean house” and restore confidence in the justice system. The Justice Department did not immediately respond. The report distinguished the February 18 instruction from termination notices sent to some prosecutors the week before and from resignations during the transition.
events.description_long: Reuters reported that Trump made the announcement in a Truth Social post, saying he wanted to “clean house” and restore confidence in the justice system. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment. The White House had sent termination notices to several Biden-appointed U.S. attorneys the week before, while others had announced resignations or left government. Reuters noted that turnover among U.S. attorneys is customary after a change in administration, though the usual practice is to request resignations rather than issue termination letters. The article separately reported that dozens of career Justice Department employees in cities including Washington and New York had been fired or quit since Trump took office; career staff are distinct from presidentially appointed U.S. attorneys. This supports a dated instruction concerning remaining Biden-appointed prosecutors, not the entry’s claim that Trump fired all U.S. attorneys and replaced them with loyalists overnight. No list of replacements is established by this source.

frozen_original.title: Trump Calls Baltic State Leaders 'All the Same' During White House Visit
frozen_original.synopsis: During a April 2018 White House meeting with the leaders of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania — three NATO allies whose independence is most directly threatened by Russian aggression — Trump reportedly told his aides the three Baltic leaders were 'all the same' and needed minimal differentiated attention, reflecting his persistent indifference to the alliance commitments most critical to European security vis-a-vis Russia. The Baltic leaders had sought the meeting specifically to obtain reassurances of Article 5 commitment following Trump's repeated public questioning of NATO's mutual defense obligations. The episode was one of multiple instances in which Trump's dismissiveness toward eastern European allies contrasted starkly with his solicitude toward Vladimir Putin. National Security Council staff reportedly worked to compensate for Trump's personal disengagement by providing robust policy-level reassurances to the Baltic capitals.

corrected_draft.description_long:
On January 30, 2017, President Trump fired Acting Attorney General Sally Yates after she ordered Justice Department lawyers not to defend the Muslim travel ban executive order in court. Yates had determined the ban was not lawful and refused to implement it, sending a letter to DOJ attorneys explaining her position. Trump responded by dismissing her within hours, calling her a 'betrayer' of the DOJ in a statement. The firing was widely condemned as an attack on the independence of the Justice Department. Yates's stand was later vindicated as courts across the country issued injunctions blocking the ban.

The conflict concerned the government's legal defense of an executive order: Yates directed department lawyers not to defend it, and Trump removed her from the acting leadership position. Her assessment of legality and subsequent court injunctions are related but distinct decisions by different institutions. The dismissal illustrates the tension between an administration's policy direction and its lawyers' obligations in court. It does not mean that every later version of the travel restrictions received the same legal treatment.

events.title: Colorado Lawsuit Cites White House Email as Evidence of Coordination
events.description_short: Colorado’s lawsuit cited a White House email as evidence for its allegation that the administration coordinated actions against the state.
events.description_medium: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser’s lawsuit accused the Trump administration of coordinating actions against the state. Denver7 and CBS Colorado reported that lawyers cited a White House email inviting officials from several agencies to discuss actions concerning Colorado. State attorneys called it evidence of coordination; the court had not determined that the email proved the allegation.
events.description_long: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser’s lawsuit accused the Trump administration of coordinating actions to punish the state. During discovery, state attorneys highlighted an email sent at 2:43 a.m. on December 15 by White House official Emily Underwood. CBS Colorado reported that the message asked officials from several departments—including Transportation, Agriculture, Interior, and Energy, as well as the Office of Management and Budget—to join a call later that day. Colorado’s lawyers called the email a “smoking gun” because they argued it showed coordination at the White House. The email was evidence cited by one side in pending litigation; a court had not determined that it proved an orchestrated campaign. The case therefore concerned both the state’s allegations and the administration’s actions across multiple agencies. The reporting supplies a concrete piece of the record behind the lawsuit, while leaving the legal claims and meaning of the email for the court to assess. The existing description’s broad conclusions should remain attributed to the state’s claims rather than treated as established findings.

corrected_draft.description_short: Whistleblower Alleges Political Pressure in Antisemitism Probes
corrected_draft.description_medium: An AP report said former Justice Department attorney Haley Van Erem’s whistleblower complaint accused the administration’s antisemitism task force of pushing settlements with Brown, Harvard and Columbia before investigations supported them. The complaint alleged Brown investigators found no Title VI violation, Columbia’s review was rushed, and Harvard settlement terms were discussed before its investigation concluded. These are allegations, not court or agency findings.
corrected_draft.description_long: The Associated Press reported that Haley Van Erem, a former Justice Department lawyer who worked on the administration’s antisemitism investigations, submitted a whistleblower complaint seeking watchdog review of the task force’s conduct. Her complaint, as described by AP, alleged that the work was marked by procedural irregularities and that officials pursued settlements before the investigations had established legal violations. At Brown, Van Erem said investigators did not find evidence of a Title VI violation, but department leadership rejected a no-violation notice and sought a settlement. At Columbia, the complaint said the inquiry moved on an accelerated schedule before the evidence and legal analysis were complete. For Harvard, it alleged officials discussed funding freezes and broad settlement terms before completing an investigation that could establish a Title VI violation. The account attributes each claim to the whistleblower complaint; it does not establish that the allegations have been independently substantiated or adjudicated. The allegations concern how federal civil-rights enforcement was conducted under the task force, not a finding that the universities did or did not violate Title VI.

events.title: Trump Promotes Census Analysis Claiming Noncitizen Votes in 2020
events.description_short: Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis claiming noncitizens voted in 2020; experts questioned its methods and said the figure could not change the result.
events.description_medium: On August 20, 2026, Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis claiming that about 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election and said it supported his claim that he won. Votebeat reported that election experts questioned the analysis because it omitted authors, detailed methods, and a margin of error. The outlet said the number, even if accurate, would not have changed the result. The Census Bureau did not respond to its request for comment.
events.description_long: On August 20, 2026, President Donald Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis that claimed, with high confidence, that approximately 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 presidential election. He said the result supported his repeated assertion that he had won that election. Votebeat reported that experts questioned the study's reliability because it did not identify its authors, explain the data's reliability in detail, or provide a margin of error. The analysis reportedly matched voter files with federal immigration records, and the data provider said it was surprised to see its files used for this purpose. The reported 24,000 figure represented less than 0.019% of the more than 128 million voters examined. Votebeat noted that even if the number were accurate, it was too small to change the outcome; it also said the analysis could not determine whether those voters supported Trump or Joe Biden. The Census Bureau did not respond to the outlet's request for comment. These distinctions matter: the report describes a government analysis and a presidential claim, alongside expert concerns about methodology. It does not establish that noncitizen voting affected the 2020 result.

A spokesperson for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said any review of trade arrangements should respect EU-U.S. agreements and international law; the European Commission said it would protect the EU’s interests because trade policy is handled for all 27 member states at the bloc level. corrected_draft.description_long: On December 20, 2025, The Associated Press reported that at least 16 files had disappeared from the Justice Department’s public webpage for Epstein-related documents less than a day after they were posted. One of the missing items was a photograph showing Donald Trump. The department did not explain the removals that day. It said on social media that photographs and other materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted as it received additional information. The removals came during publication of a large document release required by federal law. The following day, DOJ restored the Trump photograph after officials determined that no victims appeared in it, according to Reuters. Together, the reports support a description of a temporary removal and restoration of that image, and AP’s reported count of at least 16 absent files. They do not identify the full set of files or say that every file was restored. Nor do they establish that DOJ used an audit process to track the disclosure. The original title’s characterization of the episode as an ongoing, auditable exposure therefore exceeds the documented facts.

frozen_original.synopsis: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who also chairs the National Energy Dominance Council, defended aggressive fossil fuel production on public lands throughout summer 2026. A March 2026 oil and gas lease sale in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska generated $164 million — making history as the largest revenue, most tracts receiving bids, and second-most acreage sold in a single sale. The Working Families Tax Cut Act reduced the onshore royalty rate from 16.67% to 12.5%, projected to facilitate 225 additional leases in 2026. Ranking Democrat Rosa DeLauro stated: "The future this administration envisions is one of fewer national parks, shrinking public lands, more endangered species, dirtier air and water and higher profits for fossil fuel executives." Burgum called the energy transition a "fantasy" while EPA simultaneously gutted climate regulations.

child_drafts.description_long: On March 18, 2026, the Interior Department held an oil and gas lease sale in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. Those actions provide context but are distinct from this single-day auction. The page does not support the original card’s unrelated royalty-rate or congressional-criticism claims.

draft.title: Trump orders a second U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement
draft.description_short: Trump orders a second U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement
draft.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to notify the United Nations of its intent to leave the Paris Agreement, repeating his first-term withdrawal decision. The order started the treaty’s withdrawal process; it did not make the exit effective on signing day.
draft.description_long: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations to submit formal notice that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Agreement. It was the second time Trump had ordered a withdrawal: during his first term, the United States left the accord, and President Joe Biden later rejoined it in 2021. The 2025 order again reversed that policy and set a withdrawal process in motion; signing the order did not make the international withdrawal effective that same day. The Paris Agreement is the framework through which participating countries submit climate goals and report on efforts to limit warming. Leaving it reduces the United States’ participation in that shared process, although domestic emissions policy is also shaped by separate federal and state actions. This account focuses on the executive order and its diplomatic direction, rather than asserting unverified effects on other countries’ commitments or on U.S. emissions.

draft.title: OPM proposes Schedule Policy/Career rule covering an estimated 50,000 roles
draft.description_short: OPM proposed Schedule Policy/Career; White House estimated 50,000 roles could eventually qualify.
draft.description_medium: On April 18, 2025, the White House said OPM had proposed a Schedule Policy/Career rule for policy-influencing career roles. The administration estimated that 50,000 positions might eventually qualify. The proposal did not itself transfer any employee into the category; future movement depended on a final rule and later executive action.
draft.description_long: The White House fact sheet said OPM estimated that 50,000 positions, about 2 percent of the federal workforce, could ultimately be moved into Schedule Policy/Career. It also stated that the proposed rule did not itself move any positions; transfers would occur only through a later executive order after a final rule. The category was described as career positions filled through existing merit-based hiring, with employees expected to implement the law and administration policies. The fact sheet said covered roles could lose access to some adverse-action procedures and appeals, while line employees such as Border Patrol agents and wage-and-hour inspectors would generally be excluded. This was an OPM proposal and estimate, not evidence that 50,000 employees had already been reclassified or that an actual list of “disloyal” workers had been created. The narrow event is the administration’s April 18 announcement of the proposed rule.

draft.title: DOJ Drops AI-Investment Divestiture Proposal in Google Search Case
draft.description_short: DOJ dropped its proposal to require Google to sell AI investments, while continuing to seek a Chrome sale and other remedies in the search-monopoly case.
draft.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department dropped its proposal to require Google to sell its investments in AI companies, including Anthropic. DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued to seek a Chrome divestiture and other remedies in the search case. This was a change to proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case; the record’s donor-causality claim is unsupported.
draft.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice withdrew one element of its proposed remedies in the federal search-monopoly case against Google: it no longer asked the court to require Google to sell its investments in artificial-intelligence companies, including Anthropic. Reuters reported that prosecutors said evidence gathered after an earlier draft proposal indicated that a forced sale could have unintended consequences in the developing AI sector. DOJ and a coalition of 38 state attorneys general continued to seek a court order requiring Google to sell its Chrome browser and to adopt other measures addressing the search monopoly the court had found. Prosecutors also proposed advance notice to the government of future generative-AI investments. The March action therefore changed one remedy proposal; it did not drop or scale back the antitrust case as a whole. The supplied reporting does not establish that campaign or inauguration donations caused this litigation decision.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens North Korea with 'Fire and Fury'
frozen_original.synopsis: On August 8, 2017, Trump warned North Korea that any further threats would be met with 'fire and fury like the world has never seen' — improvised language evoking nuclear annihilation that alarmed military officials, allies, and arms control experts. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson immediately tried to tamp down the rhetoric by assuring Americans they could 'sleep well at night.' Former diplomats warned the language could cause North Korea to miscalculate and take pre-emptive military action. The episode revealed Trump's willingness to freelance on nuclear threats without institutional review.

corrected_draft.description_long:
Amid escalating tensions over North Korea's nuclear weapons testing, President Trump delivered an impromptu and bellicose threat on August 8, 2017, stating that further threats to the US would be met with 'fire and fury like the world has never seen.' The inflammatory rhetoric, delivered off-the-cuff from his golf club in New Jersey, shocked allies and defense experts who feared it could inadvertently trigger a nuclear conflict. The administration engaged in months of brinkmanship, with Trump frequently taunting leader Kim Jong-un as 'Little Rocket Man' before eventually pivoting to holding historic, yet largely fruitless, summits with the dictator.

The statement was a public threat made during an exchange of warnings, rather than an announcement that the United States had begun a nuclear attack. Its significance lay in the escalation risk identified by observers and the uncertainty about how the North Korean government would respond. The later turn toward meetings with Kim was a different phase of the relationship. Keeping those phases distinct allows an account of threatening rhetoric without suggesting the warning itself caused a war.

description_long.current:
Amid escalating tensions over North Korea's nuclear weapons testing, President Trump delivered an impromptu and bellicose threat on August 8, 2017, stating that further threats to the US would be met with 'fire and fury like the world has never seen.' The inflammatory rhetoric, delivered off-the-cuff from his golf club in New Jersey, shocked allies and defense experts who feared it could inadvertently trigger a nuclear conflict. The administration engaged in months of brinkmanship, with Trump frequently taunting leader Kim Jong-un as 'Little Rocket Man' before eventually pivoting to holding historic, yet largely fruitless, summits with the dictator.

The statement was a public threat made during an exchange of warnings, rather than an announcement that the United States had begun a nuclear attack. Its significance lay in the escalation risk identified by observers and the uncertainty about how the North Korean government would respond. The later turn toward meetings with Kim was a different phase of the relationship. Keeping those phases distinct allows an account of threatening rhetoric without suggesting the warning itself caused a war.

Harvard’s international students made up about one-quarter of its student body, and the administration’s action threatened the university’s ability to host students and scholars in F- and J-visa categories. Later presidential visa restrictions were separate actions and should be recorded separately if relevant. A later court filing records DHS’s May 28 notice of intent to withdraw the certification and a June 20 preliminary injunction against the May letter; the government later stipulated that it would not rely on the letter to revoke Harvard’s certification.

draft.title: Trump Issues Clemency Proclamation for January 6 Offenses
draft.description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump issued a proclamation pardoning many people convicted of January 6 offenses, commuting named sentences and directing dismissal of pending indictments.
draft.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a clemency proclamation concerning offenses related to January 6, 2021. The proclamation granted pardons to certain defendants, commuted the sentences of named individuals, and directed the attorney general to dismiss pending indictments. It was not a Justice Department motion to vacate every conviction, and pardons or commutations are legally distinct from vacating convictions.
draft.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a presidential proclamation addressing federal offenses related to events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The proclamation granted pardons to certain people convicted of those offenses, commuted the sentences of specifically named individuals to time served, and directed the attorney general to dismiss pending indictments. These actions were executive clemency. They were not a Department of Justice motion asking a court to vacate all January 6 convictions, and the proclamation did not describe every conviction as vacated. The proclamation commuted the sentences of 14 named defendants, including Stewart Rhodes and Joseph Biggs, to time served; it pardoned all other people convicted of offenses related to January 6. It directed the Bureau of Prisons to release those held in prison immediately and ordered the attorney general to pursue dismissal with prejudice of pending indictments. Those terms distinguish this presidential clemency action from a court motion to vacate convictions.

draft.title: State Department Orders Social Media Vetting for Visa Applicants Who Have Been to Gaza
draft.description_short: On April 17, 2025, the State Department ordered social-media vetting for visa applicants who had been in Gaza on or after January 1, 2007.
draft.description_medium: On April 17, 2025, the State Department directed U.S. diplomatic missions to conduct social-media vetting for immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants who had been in Gaza since January 1, 2007. Reuters reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed the cable. This is a narrower and better-supported event than the entry’s claim that DHS revoked visas simply for posts critical of Israel; the cable concerned screening and security review, not a blanket automatic revocation rule.
draft.description_long: On April 17, 2025, the State Department ordered U.S. diplomatic and consular posts to conduct social-media vetting for immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants who had been in the Gaza Strip on or after January 1, 2007. Reuters reported the directive from an internal cable signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The cable instructed that potentially derogatory security information found in an online review should prompt a security advisory opinion. Reuters also reported that the administration had revoked hundreds of visas in other cases and that officials had cited foreign-policy concerns involving some student visa holders. Those broader actions do not show that DHS revoked visas across the board because applicants had posted criticism of Israel. The corrected entry should identify the State Department’s Gaza-related screening directive, preserve its applicant scope and date, and avoid merging it with separate visa-revocation cases or attributing it to DHS.

Emptywheel argued that the subpoena investigation was politically retaliatory and connected it to Merchan’s family. That is the author’s interpretation, not an official finding that Skiba targeted Democrats to punish the judge. The supplied record does not name the consulting firm, reproduce the subpoena, explain what records investigators sought, or include responses from the prosecutors or the U.S. attorney. Those details are needed to evaluate the connection and the claim of retaliation. The source supports describing the reported investigation and the commentator’s criticism while leaving motive unresolved. An accessible copy of the subpoena and official responses would be necessary for a fuller account.

draft.title: OCC conditionally approves World Liberty Trust bank application
draft.description_short: OCC conditionally approves World Liberty Trust bank application
draft.description_medium: On August 18, 2026, The New Republic reported conditional OCC approval of World Liberty Financial’s application for World Liberty Trust Company, a national trust bank. The article said further requirements remained before it could open and argued the Trump family’s stake raised conflict concerns. Its legal and ethical framing is commentary; the approval did not establish misconduct or permit the bank to operate.
draft.description_long: On August 18, 2026, The New Republic reported that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency had granted preliminary conditional approval to World Liberty Financial’s application for a national trust bank called World Liberty Trust Company. The article describes a trust bank as an institution that primarily holds and manages assets rather than taking deposits or making ordinary loans. The OCC approval was not permission to open: the applicant still had to raise capital, satisfy other conditions and complete pre-opening review. The New Republic says the Trump family holds a substantial ownership stake in World Liberty Financial and receives revenue from its cryptocurrency business. It argues that the approval raises a conflict because the family could benefit from a company receiving federal banking approval under an administration led by Trump. Those ownership details and the conflict argument are claims reported in the article, not a finding of misconduct. The event is the regulator’s preliminary approval; the article’s corruption characterization is opinion. The charter process remained incomplete in the report.

The competing positions matter: the judge’s reported characterization is an assessment in the litigation, while the Pentagon continued to defend the legality of its action. The immediate consequence supported here is that the Pentagon’s blacklisting was blocked while the case proceeded; its ultimate legal resolution is not provided in the supplied account.

corrected_draft.description_long:
On September 14, 2026, the Supreme Court denied an emergency stay requested by the U.S. Postal Service in litigation over ballot-mail restrictions. The denial left an injunction against the restrictions in place. The Court's majority said the government was unlikely to succeed, while Justice Brett Kavanaugh separately stressed that there was insufficient time to implement the restrictions before the midterms.

The immediate consequence was that the injunction continued to block implementation while the litigation proceeded. The case concerned restrictions affecting ballot mail, making the timing of any change consequential in the run-up to an election. Kavanaugh's stated concern about implementation time was distinct from the majority's assessment of the government's likelihood of success; the two points should not be conflated as a single rationale.

This was an emergency stay decision, not a final ruling on the merits invalidating every possible version of the policy. It therefore should not be read as resolving all legal questions about ballot-mail restrictions or foreclosing future action under a different rule or on a fuller record. The supplied account does not detail the underlying injunction's full terms, the lower court's reasoning, or the next steps in the litigation. The decision's direct effect, as described in the supplied facts, was to leave the existing injunction in place rather than permit the Postal Service to implement the challenged restrictions at that stage.

corrected_draft.description_short: The Atlantic’s 2019 “Unthinkable” package selected 50 incidents from Trump’s first two years, according to contemporaneous reporting.
corrected_draft.description_medium: The Atlantic’s January 14, 2019 “Unthinkable” feature surveyed Trump’s first two years through 50 selected incidents. corrected_draft.description_long: The Atlantic introduced “Unthinkable” on January 14, 2019, two years into Donald Trump’s first term. In a contemporaneous Atlantic newsletter, the magazine described it as a catalog of 50 improbable incidents that it considered outlandish or destructive; one featured episode was Trump’s May 9, 2017, firing of FBI Director James Comey. In an interview that day with WBUR’s On Point, series developer and co-editor Adrienne LaFrance explained how the package was assembled. A research team examined every day of Trump’s first two years and initially identified hundreds of moments before editors narrowed the selection to 50. LaFrance said the episodes ranged from small to large and were hard to weigh individually as they happened. Looking back across the period, she saw recurring challenges to norms in Trump’s communications with the press and his treatment of institutions. The project was an editorial review of selected events and their cumulative pattern, not a quantitative measure of how readers perceived democratic risk.

It also does not establish that Ramaswamy’s Ohio policy positions were intended to benefit Strive investors, describe his other business interests, or connect this filing to a campaign decision. Those broader claims require separate sources and should not be inferred from the ownership amendment. The entry should remain limited to what the SEC document reports about share ownership and the related reporting event.

candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_short: Birthright citizenship executive order and later court injunction
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the birthright citizenship executive order on January 20, 2025. It covered births where the mother was unlawfully present, or lawfully present temporarily, and the father was neither a U.S. citizen nor lawful permanent resident; the order exempted children of lawful permanent residents. A Maryland judge issued a later nationwide injunction on August 7, Reuters reported.
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies not to recognize U.S. citizenship for certain children born in the United States. The order covered two categories: births where the mother was unlawfully present and the father was neither a U.S. citizen nor a lawful permanent resident, and births where the mother was lawfully present temporarily and the father had neither status. It expressly exempted children of lawful permanent residents and was scheduled to apply to births more than 30 days after signing. Reuters reported that a Maryland federal judge issued a class-action injunction on August 7, 2025, the fourth nationwide injunction against the policy. The signing and the injunction are separate milestones. The cited records do not establish the held synopsis’s broad “neither parent” paraphrase, an annual estimate of 150,000 affected births, or an October 3 ruling date. This proposal describes the order’s text and one later court action; it does not treat the injunction count as an order-signing fact or make a broader merits claim.

candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.title: Justice Department announces zero-tolerance prosecution policy
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_short: The Justice Department announced a zero-tolerance prosecution policy for unlawful entry at the Southwest border.
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_medium: On April 6, 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced a zero-tolerance policy directing Southwest Border U.S. Attorney’s Offices to prosecute all Department of Homeland Security referrals for unlawful-entry offenses, to the extent practicable. The release identified five districts and framed the policy as criminal enforcement; it did not expressly direct family separation.
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_long: On April 6, 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced a “zero-tolerance” policy for unlawful-entry offenses under 8 U.S.C. §1325(a). The Justice Department directed each U.S. Attorney’s Office along the Southwest Border to prosecute all Department of Homeland Security referrals under that provision, to the extent practicable. The release named five affected districts: Southern California, Arizona, New Mexico, Western Texas and Southern Texas, and framed the action as federal criminal enforcement. The announcement establishes the prosecution policy and its date. Bannon was facing federal charges related to the We Build the Wall fundraising effort, in which prosecutors accused him of defrauding supporters; he had pleaded not guilty. The clemency came before the criminal case reached trial. The record should describe the charges as allegations and should not imply a conviction or a finding that donations were misused. The reviewed Reuters report establishes the grant, its date and Bannon’s pending case status. It does not establish whether Bannon applied through the Office of the Pardon Attorney, so the claim that he filed no petition should be omitted. This entry documents a specific clemency action, not the later disposition of the charges or the merits of the fundraising allegations.

latest_supported_candidate.title: Trump Urges Supreme Court to Limit Nationwide Injunctions
latest_supported_candidate.description_short: On March 20, 2025, Trump urged the Supreme Court to curtail federal judges’ power to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration actions.
latest_supported_candidate.description_medium: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump urged the Supreme Court to curtail federal judges’ ability to issue nationwide injunctions against administration actions. Reuters reported that Trump posted “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW” and that the Justice Department had asked the Court to narrow injunctions blocking his birthright-citizenship order. This supports a specific challenge to nationwide injunctions, not a claim that Trump denied courts all authority over the executive branch.
latest_supported_candidate.description_long: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump called on the Supreme Court to limit federal judges’ authority to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration policies. Reuters reported that Trump made the appeal in a social-media post, writing “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW,” and that the Justice Department was separately asking the justices to narrow three nationwide injunctions against his birthright-citizenship order. The cases involved courts in Washington state, Massachusetts and Maryland. Trump’s statement concerned the scope of injunctions that apply beyond the parties before a court. The available reporting does not say that he declared federal judges had no authority to constrain or review the executive branch. Reuters also reported that federal courts were hearing more than 100 lawsuits against administration initiatives and that the Supreme Court’s six-member conservative majority included three Trump appointees. Injunctions against earlier presidents had also been issued. The event should be described as a call to curtail nationwide injunctions and related Supreme Court litigation, not a rejection of judicial review generally.

latest_supported_candidate.title: Trump orders agency reviews to combat campus antisemitism
latest_supported_candidate.description_short: Trump’s January 29 order directed agencies to review existing authorities and complaints concerning campus antisemitism.
latest_supported_candidate.description_medium: On January 29, 2025, President Donald Trump directed agencies to report on existing authorities, actions and pending administrative complaints related to antisemitism at colleges and universities. The order set a 60-day reporting deadline and requested recommendations from several departments. It did not create a new offense criminalizing critics for material support of terrorism.
latest_supported_candidate.description_long: The January 29, 2025 executive order directs agency heads to report within 60 days on existing authorities or actions that could be used to combat antisemitism at colleges and universities. It also asks the Attorney General to analyze pending administrative complaints involving higher-education institutions and alleged civil-rights violations connected to antisemitism, and to inventory relevant court cases and actions taken or planned. The order encourages use of existing civil-rights enforcement tools. It separately asks the State, Education and Homeland Security departments to recommend ways for universities to identify and report certain noncitizen activity relevant to grounds of inadmissibility. These are agency-review and reporting instructions. The text does not establish a new statutory definition of material support, or authorize prosecution of critics merely for criticism, donations or association. That distinction matters because the held title described a specific criminalization order that the reviewed document does not contain. The proposal retains the order’s review and reporting function while leaving possible later enforcement actions to their own evidence and dates.

The order encourages use of existing civil-rights enforcement tools. It separately asks the State, Education and Homeland Security departments to recommend ways for universities to identify and report certain noncitizen activity relevant to grounds of inadmissibility. That distinction matters because the held title described a specific criminalization order that the reviewed document does not contain. The proposal retains the order’s review and reporting function while leaving possible later enforcement actions to their own evidence and dates.

candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.title: Ninth Circuit rejects Nevada acting U.S. attorney appointment
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_short: Ninth Circuit rejects Nevada acting U.S. attorney appointment
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_medium: On August 17, 2026, the Ninth Circuit ruled that Sigal Chattah’s Nevada acting U.S. attorney appointment bypassed Senate confirmation. The court left three indictments intact at that stage and allowed defendants to raise separate challenges in later proceedings; the decision did not automatically void those cases.
candidate_not_selected_or_blocked.description_long: On August 17, 2026, the Ninth Circuit ruled against the Trump administration’s appointment of Sigal Chattah as acting U.S. attorney in Nevada without Senate confirmation. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the court rejected an indefinite acting appointment as a way to avoid the confirmation process. The ruling left three indictments obtained while Chattah held the position intact at that stage because the appellate court could not review those prosecutions in this proceeding. Defendants remained able to raise separate challenges in later proceedings, so the decision did not dismiss or automatically invalidate the indictments. The judgment addresses Chattah’s appointment and the relief available in the appeal. It does not resolve every appointment or prosecution nationwide, and the broader claim that the court rejected all administration appointment strategy should not be inferred from this Nevada decision. For this entry, the event is the court’s ruling on the Nevada appointment; the case-specific effect on the three indictments is limited by the panel’s procedural ruling.

corrected_draft.description_long: A Reuters/Ipsos poll reported that 69% of Americans believe Donald Trump has inappropriately profited since returning to power. It also found that 63% consider it inappropriate for Trump and his family to profit from his presidency. The results capture public perceptions about the intersection of presidential office and private financial interests; they do not, by themselves, establish that a specific transaction was improper or that a law was broken. The poll was covered by GMA News Online and other outlets linked to this entry. The supplied summary does not provide the poll's field dates, sample size, question wording, or margin of error, so those methodological details cannot be assessed here. The findings nonetheless indicate substantial public concern about potential conflicts of interest involving Trump and his family. Such perceptions can shape public trust in government and scrutiny of presidential conduct, but the poll alone does not measure those effects or establish their causes. The entry records an opinion survey, not a legal finding. Its central figures should therefore be understood as respondents' reported beliefs and judgments, rather than proof of financial misconduct. Further evaluation of any particular allegation would require evidence about the underlying business activity and relevant rules, neither of which is detailed in the supplied poll summary.

corrected_draft.description_long: On September 8, 2026, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to halt a lower-court order blocking an expanded federal system that used immigration-status information to check state voter rolls. Reuters reported that Justice Department lawyers sought to restore broader citizenship screening before the midterm elections. The filing requested interim relief; it was not a decision by the Supreme Court and did not itself reinstate the database. It was also distinct from the system’s initial rollout and from later proceedings. The request raised questions about federal access to state voter information and the use of citizenship data in election administration. The lower-court judge, the legal arguments, and the number of voter records that could be checked are not specified here. The filing does not establish that the system identified ineligible voters. Its significance is the administration’s effort to revive a challenged screening tool during an election period, while the court’s response and the tool’s accuracy remain separate questions.

The linked SCOTUSblog account reports the order and the dissenting justices. children.title: Court Sets Aside HUD's 2025 Continuum of Care Funding Notices
children.description_short: A federal court ruled that HUD's November and December 2025 Continuum of Care notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act and set them aside.
children.description_medium: On June 29, 2026, a federal court set aside HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices. California’s attorney general said the ruling found the notices unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act and preserved billions in homelessness funding. This decision concerned FY2025 notices; the separate August 2026 ruling addressed a later FY2026 notice.
children.description_long: A federal court ruled on June 29, 2026 that HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices could not stand. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found that HUD had made material changes to the program without following the Administrative Procedure Act. The ruling set aside the notices and preserved approximately $3.6 billion in funding for homelessness programs while litigation proceeded. The Continuum of Care program funds local and regional systems that coordinate housing and services for people experiencing homelessness. The June decision concerned the prior fiscal year’s competition and its funding notices. It should be described as a court ruling about those particular notices, rather than a blanket reversal of all HUD policy changes or a finding on every asserted consequence for people in permanent supportive housing. A later, separate August 2026 decision addressed HUD’s FY2026 notice and should retain its own date and procedural posture.

children.description_medium: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked HUD’s FY2026 Continuum of Care notice changes. California’s attorney general reported that the court found the policy revisions unlawful and preserved permanent supportive housing funding. HUD’s program page confirms the program’s annual competition context; the court ruling remains a separate action from the June decision about FY2025 notices.
children.description_long: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked changes HUD had made to the FY2026 Continuum of Care funding competition. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found the administration’s revisions unlawful and prevented the new notice from diverting funds away from permanent supportive housing. HUD describes Continuum of Care as a competitive program that supports community systems serving people experiencing homelessness. The August ruling concerned the FY2026 notice and followed a June ruling that set aside HUD’s earlier FY2025 notices. These are separate court orders involving different annual funding competitions; they should not be collapsed into one ruling or described as three separate wins without identifying the orders. The state release characterizes the result as protecting permanent supportive housing, while the HUD competition page supplies the administrative program context. The available sources do not establish the held claim that exactly 97,000 people would be pushed onto the street.

children.description_short: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed orders directing the department to review policies that burden energy development and identify authorities to expedite permitting and leasing.
children.description_medium: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed six departmental orders, including SO 3418, directing reviews of policies considered burdensome to energy development and encouraging production on federal lands and waters. children.description_long: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed six departmental orders, including Secretarial Order 3418, “Unleashing American Energy.” Interior’s announcement says the orders directed review of actions that could burden energy development and promotion of energy production on federal lands and waters. The department’s order page identifies the order and links its signed text. This account concerns the issuance of review directives; it does not establish that every review was completed or that every permitting timeline changed. The cited documents do not establish the original account’s 28-day general permitting deadline, acreage near Yellowstone or Grand Teton, or overlap with wildlife migration corridors. Those claims should not be attached to this action. BLM’s June 2026 Wyoming sale is a separate event with its own reported acreage and proceeds. A separate sale result should be described only with the agency’s final acreage and receipt figures, not treated as an effect of the February order.

children.title: BLM leases about 114,439 Wyoming acres in quarterly oil and gas sale
children.description_short: BLM reported leasing 102 parcels totaling about 114,439 acres in its June 2026 Wyoming oil and gas sale for $34.7 million in receipts.
children.description_medium: BLM reported that its June 9, 2026 Wyoming oil-and-gas sale leased 102 parcels totaling about 114,439 acres and generated $34.7 million in receipts. The agency release supports this sale’s acreage and proceeds, but not the original claims about nearby migration corridors or a different proposed auction.
children.description_long: On June 9, 2026, the Bureau of Land Management held a quarterly oil-and-gas lease sale in Wyoming. BLM reported that 102 parcels covering approximately 114,439 acres were leased, generating total receipts of $34,706,638. The agency said combined lease bonus bids and rentals are distributed between the federal government and the state where parcels are located. This is a completed sale and its reported acreage and proceeds can be stated directly with attribution to BLM. The release does not establish the original card’s assertions about the sale being near Yellowstone, overlap with state-designated mule-deer or pronghorn migration corridors, or the terms of a separate proposed auction. Those claims concern distinct land parcels or future offerings and require separate maps, sale notices, or environmental records. The June sale should therefore be described as its own event, with location, number of parcels, acreage and proceeds drawn from the BLM announcement rather than generalized to all 2026 Wyoming leasing.

Sloman, former second-in-command to U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta, stated in documents released by House Oversight that the 2008 Epstein non-prosecution agreement was structured in secret, and specifically references Donald Trump and other senior officials among those who exerted pressure to secure the lenient deal. The Sloman documents represent the most direct allegation that Trump personally influenced the deal that kept Epstein out of federal prison for a decade.

children.title: Trump orders U.S. withdrawal process from the World Health Organization
children.description_short: Trump orders U.S. withdrawal process from the World Health Organization.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to begin withdrawing from the World Health Organization. It directed officials to pause future U.S. funding, recall or reassign U.S. personnel and contractors, and suspend negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement while withdrawal proceeded. The order began a withdrawal process; it did not immediately end U.S. membership.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to begin withdrawing from the World Health Organization. The order instructed the Secretary of State and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to pause future transfers of U.S. government funds to WHO, recall and reassign U.S. personnel and contractors working with the organization, and suspend negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement. It also directed officials to identify alternative partners for relevant public-health activities. The order initiated a withdrawal process under the organization’s notice requirements; it did not immediately remove the United States from WHO on the day it was signed. The later decision to withdraw from UNESCO was made in a separate July 2025 announcement and under a different international organization’s procedures. The original combined title therefore conflates two actions separated by six months and involving distinct institutions.

corrected_draft.description_short: Trump administration announces DACA rescission plan

corrected_draft.description_long: The Trump administration announced in September 2017 that it would rescind Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, the DACA program created in 2012 to defer deportation for eligible people brought to the United States as children. Attorney General Jeff Sessions called the program unlawful and gave Congress a six-month window to pass a legislative replacement. The announcement put roughly 700,000 recipients at risk of losing work authorization and protection from removal, but court orders blocked the rescission while lawsuits proceeded. In June 2020, the Supreme Court ruled that the administration had acted arbitrarily and capriciously because it had not adequately considered the consequences and alternatives. The Court did not resolve every question about presidential authority over DACA. The program therefore was not terminated on the 2017 announcement date and remained operative for eligible recipients during the litigation. The sequence shows the difference between announcing a rescission and carrying it out after judicial review.

record.title: Trump threatens to revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status
record.description_short: Trump said his administration would revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status; Harvard called the threat unlawful and unprecedented.
record.description_medium: On May 2, 2025, Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard’s tax-exempt status. Reuters described it as a renewed threat after a similar April 15 post. Harvard called revocation unlawful and unprecedented. The university was already challenging a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. Reuters also described government demands on governance and viewpoints; no revocation was reported.
record.description_long: On May 2, 2025, President Donald Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard University’s tax-exempt status. Reuters reported that Trump gave no explanation in that post and described it as a renewed threat following a similar statement on April 15. Harvard responded that revocation would be unlawful and unprecedented, and said there was no legal basis to rescind its status. At the time, Harvard was already suing over a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. Reuters also reported that the university had faced demands concerning governance, faculty and student viewpoints, masks, and diversity initiatives after rejecting the administration’s terms. The article distinguishes Trump’s threat from an actual IRS revocation: IRS representatives did not respond to Reuters’ questions, and the White House said any IRS action would be independent. The record should therefore describe a public threat directed at Harvard on May 2, not a completed tax-status change or a February action against multiple universities.

The Government Accountability Office issued findings that multiple redirections were illegal impoundments. Federal courts issued injunctions in several cases blocking the fund transfers. The actions were seen as a systematic attempt to make the executive branch independent of congressional spending authority.

record.title: Trump Revokes Federal Contractor Affirmative-Action Order
record.description_short: On January 21, 2025, Trump revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed changes to federal contractor affirmative-action requirements, with a 90-day transition period.
record.description_medium: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, which revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed the Labor Department’s contractor-compliance office to cease promoting diversity and holding contractors responsible for affirmative action. The order allowed contractors to continue following the prior regulatory scheme for 90 days. It was signed January 21, not January 20.
record.description_long: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity.” The order revoked Executive Order 11246, which had governed equal employment opportunity requirements for federal contractors. It directed the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs to cease promoting diversity and holding federal contractors and subcontractors responsible for affirmative action. The order also required federal contracts and grants to include terms concerning compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws and certifications about unlawful DEI programs. For 90 days, contractors could continue complying with the regulatory scheme that had been in effect on January 20. The title should therefore identify the January 21 order and its contractor provisions rather than claim that every contracting requirement ended on January 20. The White House text is primary evidence of the order’s date and terms; broader implementation effects are outside this event description.

corrected_draft.description_long: A 2026 investigation by ProPublica reported that federal officials were searching for criminal cases to support President Donald Trump's claims that noncitizen voting was tipping elections. Homeland Security Investigations agents pursued leads across the country, including hundreds in Minnesota. On March 24, a Justice Department official demanded a quick status report from the Minnesota U.S. attorney's office, whose staff said they had subpoenaed records on about 130 people and referred only one person for prosecution. The reporting also described pressure on the office to treat the cases as a high priority and an extraordinary demand for approval before declining to proceed. Local election offices received calls and record requests from agents. The investigation found that noncitizen voting is rare and that people can appear on voter rolls through administrative errors without casting ballots. The results undercut claims that widespread illegal voting by noncitizens was changing election outcomes. The effort raised questions about using federal investigative powers to pursue a political claim when the cases reviewed produced little evidence of prosecutable voting violations. The episode documents an investigation and referral count; it does not establish that the one referral resulted in a conviction.

corrected_draft.description_long: Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court to let construction of a proposed White House ballroom continue while a legal challenge proceeded. Two lower courts had ruled that the project was moving forward without congressional authorization. Trump’s emergency request sought permission to keep building without restrictions; an appeals court order blocking most above-ground work was due to take effect August 21 unless the Supreme Court intervened. The planned addition was described as about 90,000 square feet, larger than the White House mansion and West Wing combined, with a security bunker beneath it. Trump had demolished the East Wing to make way for the structure. Related reporting described the underground facilities as a military complex, while Trump called opponents of the ballroom disloyal to the country. The dispute placed the construction project before the justices on an urgent schedule. The request was not itself a Supreme Court ruling, and the reports do not establish the eventual outcome of the emergency application.

record.description_medium: In his August 20, 2026 New York Review of Books essay on Regime Change, Mark Danner describes Trump’s second-term governing style as a “constitutional dictatorship.” He links the argument to expansive executive power and emergency declarations, while noting that political and practical costs sometimes prompted retreats. The phrase is his interpretation, not a court finding or formal legal status.
record.description_long: Mark Danner’s August 20, 2026 essay in the New York Review of Books reviews Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s book Regime Change and calls Trump’s second-term governing style a “constitutional dictatorship.” Danner argues that Trump expanded executive power by invoking emergencies and weakening Congress’s role, and uses the book’s reporting to discuss tariffs, immigration enforcement and other policies. He also notes occasions when Trump backed down after markets fell, courts intervened or political costs rose. The phrase is the essayist’s political characterization; it is not a court finding, legal status or description of one discrete order. The essay offers commentary on several actions and responses rather than a single event. The packet’s duplicate records carry different stored dates but cite this same NYRB essay, published on August 20. A publication-context summary should identify that essay and its argument without presenting Danner’s assessment as an established legal conclusion.

corrected_draft.description_long.current: A federal lawsuit filed in the Southern District of New York on August 12, 2026, accused the Trump administration of violating the First Amendment by selling advance access to Truth Social posts. The plaintiffs were the Freedom of the Press Foundation and The Intercept, represented by several legal organizations. Their complaint challenged Truth API, a service announced by Truth Social’s parent company that offered early access to posts by Trump and other officials for as much as $100,000 per month; the report said at least 10 customers had signed up. The plaintiffs argued that the president was monetizing public statements and providing market-moving government information to paying users. The report noted that Trump held a 41% stake in Trump Media & Technology Group through a trust controlled by one of his sons, and that the administration had treated his Truth Social posts as official presidential statements in other contexts. These are allegations in a newly filed case, not a court ruling. The White House had not responded to the request for comment when the report was published.

The linked fact-checks document those issues, but their assessment should not be overstated as proof that the United States could not fight or that every claimed diplomatic outcome was false. corrected_draft.description_short: AP reported that 16 Epstein-related files briefly disappeared from the Justice Department’s public repository.
corrected_draft.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that 16 files related to Jeffrey Epstein briefly disappeared from a Justice Department public repository. Coverage also said a photograph was temporarily removed for review. The reports document a temporary change in what the public repository displayed; they do not establish that files were permanently suppressed or explain intent beyond the department’s stated review. The original implication of deliberate concealment should therefore be removed unless additional records establish it.
corrected_draft.description_long: The Associated Press reported on December 20, 2025, that at least 16 files related to Jeffrey Epstein had briefly disappeared from a Justice Department public repository. NPR’s coverage also described a photograph that the department said had been temporarily removed for review. These reports support a limited account of files becoming unavailable and later attention to the repository’s contents. They do not show that the files were permanently deleted, establish who made each change, or prove an effort to conceal evidence. The distinction matters because a temporary removal for review and a deliberate, lasting suppression are different claims. A corrected description should attribute the count and the explanation to the reporting, retain the short duration where the reports specify it, and avoid assigning motive without direct documentation. The source record is evidence of a reported repository change, not proof of a broader cover-up.

latest_supported_candidate.description_short: CREW counted 191 days with Trump property visits in his first 512 days back in office, or 37%; the analysis does not substantiate the held entry’s $115 million cost total.
latest_supported_candidate.description_medium: A June 16, 2026 CREW analysis said Donald Trump had visited properties he owns on 191 of his first 512 days back in office, or 37%. The article lists 102 visits to Mar-a-Lago and says Secret Service records showed nearly $100,000 spent at Trump properties in the first few months of the second term. It notes that the amount excludes costs from other agencies and discusses Air Force One operating costs by citing a Palm Beach Post analysis. The article does not establish the held entry’s $115 million cumulative travel-and-security figure or its $300 million end-of-term projection. Those totals need a separate auditable source and methodology.

latest_supported_candidate.title: Supreme Court clears path for possible dismissal of Bannon contempt case
latest_supported_candidate.description_short: On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the appeals court ruling upholding Steve Bannon’s contempt conviction and remanded the case.
latest_supported_candidate.description_medium: Reuters reported that DOJ told the justices dismissal was in the interests of justice and had already filed a dismissal motion in the trial court. Bannon had been convicted in 2022 after defying a congressional subpoena and served a four-month sentence in 2024. The Supreme Court docket lists a February 9, 2026 filing by the United States.
latest_supported_candidate.description_long: Steve Bannon was convicted in 2022 on two counts of contempt of Congress for refusing to provide documents or testimony to the House committee investigating the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The D.C. Circuit upheld his conviction in May 2024, and the Supreme Court denied his request to remain out of prison while appealing in June 2024. Bannon served a four-month federal prison sentence later that year. On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the appellate judgment and remanded the matter. Reuters reported that DOJ told the Court dismissal was in the interests of justice and had already filed a dismissal motion in district court. The remand returned the case to the trial court for further proceedings; DOJ’s motion still required judicial action. The appellate judgment was vacated; the Supreme Court did not itself enter a dismissal. This account is limited to the procedural action and the government’s reported position.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends FEMA National Flood Insurance Program
frozen_original.synopsis: In 2025, the Trump administration moved to effectively wind down the Federal Emergency Management Agency's National Flood Insurance Program, which provides flood coverage to millions of homeowners in flood-prone areas where private insurance is unavailable or unaffordable. The program provides coverage to approximately five million policyholders in coastal and riverside communities that face mounting flood risks worsened by climate change. Real estate markets in Florida, Louisiana, and the Gulf Coast faced significant disruption as lenders began requiring more expensive private flood coverage or refusing mortgages. Mayors and governors from both parties objected, warning of cascading economic damage to their regions. Critics noted the policy was most harmful to residents of states that had strongly supported Trump.

latest_supported_candidate.title: Trump says he will always abide by courts during funding-freeze case
latest_supported_candidate.description_short: Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” as an appeals court rejected an emergency request in the funding-freeze dispute.
latest_supported_candidate.description_medium: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” while the administration challenged a lower-court order blocking a broad federal funding freeze. The First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate stay and left the district court to clarify the order’s scope. This records the February assurance; it does not support the original March claim that Trump said he could override court orders.
latest_supported_candidate.description_long: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” during a dispute over the administration’s effort to freeze federal funding. That day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate administrative stay of a lower-court order blocking the broad freeze. The appellate panel said it was uncertain what standards governed the requested stay and noted that the administration had not cited authority supporting it. The court left the district judge to clarify the scope of the earlier order and said it would consider a later request for a stay pending appeal. ABC reported that the administration argued the order improperly constrained executive spending authority, while state plaintiffs said a renewed freeze would harm recipients of federal funding. Trump’s brief assurance was made in this litigation context. It contradicts the held card’s claim that he declared he was not bound by court orders; the evidence supports recording the February statement and court response, not the alleged March declaration.

proposal.description_long: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” during a dispute over the administration’s effort to freeze federal funding. That day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate administrative stay of a lower-court order blocking the broad freeze. The appellate panel said it was uncertain what standards governed the requested stay and noted that the administration had not cited authority supporting it. The court left the district judge to clarify the scope of the earlier order and said it would consider a later request for a stay pending appeal. ABC reported that the administration argued the order improperly constrained executive spending authority, while state plaintiffs said a renewed freeze would harm recipients of federal funding. Trump’s brief assurance was made in this litigation context. It contradicts the held card’s claim that he declared he was not bound by court orders; the evidence supports recording the February statement and court response, not the alleged March declaration.
